content.overview: BNS s. 20 — Act of a child under seven years of age.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
A child under seven years is doli incapax — conclusively deemed incapable of committing an offence. No evidence of maturity can take this away.
In student language: BNS s. 20 is the rule on “Act of a child under seven years of age”. The section provides that nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 20 exists so that “Act of a child under seven years of age” has a closed legal test in Chapter III — General Exceptions. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: When an act is not an offence: mistake, accident, infancy, unsoundness, consent, compulsion — and the right of private defence.

The provision in detail
20. Nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age

Essential ingredients
1. Nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age

Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:

Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 20 in a vacuum.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 20 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

learningObjectives: State the age condition in BNS s.20.
Apply the rule that nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age.
Distinguish absolute immunity under seven from the qualified child rule that follows in the next section.
enhancement.definition: BNS s.20 provides that nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Section 20 is an age-based general exception. It does not ask about maturity, understanding, or the nature of the act. The only statutory condition in this section is that the child is under seven years of age.
statutoryFramework: Chapter III — General Exceptions, BNS s.20.
The actor is a child under seven years of age.
If that age condition is met, nothing is an offence by reason of this section.
The next section, BNS s.21, is the separate qualified rule for a child above seven and under twelve who has not attained sufficient maturity. Do not merge the two tests.
No illustration is printed in the migrated s.20 text.
essentialIngredients: The person who does the act is a child.
The child is under seven years of age at the time of the act.
No further mental-element enquiry is written into s.20.
If the child is seven or older, s.20 does not apply.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 20 is short and should be applied as written. The section does not grade the act and does not require proof that the child lacked understanding. Age under seven is the condition. A problem answer should identify the date of the act and the child's age on that date. A child who has turned seven is outside this section even if the child is still very young; the qualified maturity rule, if it is to be used, is the next section and must be argued separately. This exception is not a defence of accident, necessity or mistake. It is a status exception. No case name is added here. The migrated topic has no printed statutory illustration, so a teaching example should be labelled as an example.
examples: Teaching example: a child aged six takes property from a shop. Section 20 says nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven. The age condition is the point to prove.
Teaching example: the same child does the act on the seventh birthday. Section 20 no longer applies. Do not invent a maturity finding to keep s.20 alive.
Teaching example: a child aged ten. Section 20 fails on age. Any further argument belongs to the above-seven and under-twelve section, not to s.20.
distinctions: Section 20 is absolute for a child under seven. It does not contain a maturity test.
Section 21, not s.20, deals with a child above seven and under twelve who has not attained sufficient maturity of understanding.
Infancy is not accident under s.18 and not necessity under s.19.
problemApplication: Issue: whether the act is no offence under s.20.
Rule: nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age.
Application: prove age at the time of the act. If under seven, conclude. If not, leave this section.
Conclusion: do not add a mental test that the section does not write.

shortAnswer: Say the section has no maturity enquiry.
Point to the next section for a child above seven and under twelve.
tenMark: Failure example at seven or above.
Conclusion and the boundary with s.21.
sixteenMark: Introduction and why the rule is absolute.
Proof of age on the date of the act.
Contrast with the qualified child rule.

keyTakeaways: Under seven, s.20 says nothing is an offence.
The section does not ask whether the child understood the act.
Seven or older is outside s.20.
